No page that answered names DDR4-2666 as a platform grade -- the Ice Lake-SP tables only ever show 2933 and 3200 -- so this grade is carried over from the previous round unconfirmed.

Capacity variant of the same grade. Module capacity does not change the clock at a given DIMM-per-channel count -- speed is a property of the DDR grade and the population, which is what the cited source states and what effective_mts records. 16 GB RDIMMs are a standard server SKU and are the cheapest way to populate every channel on an 8- or 12-channel board, which is what actually determines bandwidth. Rank count (1Rx8 vs 2Rx8) is not modelled: it can matter at 2 DIMMs per channel, so treat 2DPC figures for this capacity as the same first-order estimate as the rest of the table.

Capacity variant of the same grade; see the 16 GB row for why capacity does not change the clock. 8 GB RDIMMs are the floor for filling every channel cheaply -- eight of them fill an 8-channel board for 64 GB, which is enough for a 7B model at Q4 and gives full bandwidth. They are single-rank, so bank parallelism is lower than a 2-rank module of the same grade; that effect is not modelled here and would make these slightly optimistic.

STILL UNVERIFIED, and deliberately so: this row's load-bearing number is the 2-DIMM-per-channel derate (2666 -> 2666 MT/s), and no source that answered publishes it. Intel's platform and memory-population pages return HTTP 403, and the Wikipedia SKU tables give one memory grade per SKU with no DIMM-population qualifier -- they cannot express a 2DPC figure at all. The only 2DPC fact obtained this round is that Sapphire Rapids supports up to 2 DIMMs per channel ("8-channel DDR5 ECC memory support up to DDR5-4800, up to 2 DIMMs per channel", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphire_Rapids), not what it clocks at. The derate is therefore carried over from the previous round. The table is also keyed only by DDR generation, so it cannot express per-platform differences -- most notably EPYC Genoa derates further than Intel at 2DPC. Confirm against the server OEM's memory population rules before quoting.

Capacity variant of the same grade. Module capacity does not change the clock at a given DIMM-per-channel count -- speed is a property of the DDR grade and the population, which is what the cited source states and what effective_mts records. 16 GB RDIMMs are a standard server SKU and are the cheapest way to populate every channel on an 8- or 12-channel board, which is what actually determines bandwidth. Rank count (1Rx8 vs 2Rx8) is not modelled: it can matter at 2 DIMMs per channel, so treat 2DPC figures for this capacity as the same first-order estimate as the rest of the table.

Capacity variant of the same grade; see the 16 GB row for why capacity does not change the clock. 8 GB RDIMMs are the floor for filling every channel cheaply -- eight of them fill an 8-channel board for 64 GB, which is enough for a 7B model at Q4 and gives full bandwidth. They are single-rank, so bank parallelism is lower than a 2-rank module of the same grade; that effect is not modelled here and would make these slightly optimistic.
